intro.title: Measuring extraction.
intro.lead: You will pull the same fields out of four contracts, and then answer a harder question: how often was it right? Not "does that look correct". A number.
intro.teach: You will pull the same fields out of four contracts, and then answer a harder question: how often was it right? Not "does that look correct". A number.

close.title: Write down what counts as correct, and the eval comes free.
close.lead: An answer key grades extraction, where one value is right. A rubric grades judgment, where several outputs could be good. Between them you can measure both halves of the work. Neither one measures the other.
close.teach: An answer key grades extraction, where one value is right. A rubric grades judgment, where several outputs could be good. Between them you can measure both halves of the work. Neither one measures the other.

steps.title: Four managed-services agreements
steps.teach: Twenty to thirty pages each, written the way a real supplier contract is written. Every sector signs these: law, accounting, financial services, personal injury.

checks.q: Why use four real-length agreements rather than one short sample?

options.t: Because the exercise takes too little time otherwise.
options.why: Filling the hour isn't a reason to do anything.

options.t: To give the model more training material.
options.why: Nothing is being trained. Think about what you're trying to find out.

options.t: Because a rate needs more than one case, and real documents fail in ways samples don't.

steps.title: Finish the schema
steps.teach: A schema is the formal definition of the data you want out. Three things for every field.

checks.q: A schema defines the data you want out. What does each field need?

options.t: A name and a data type.
options.why: Two of three. Something is missing that decides whether an answer counts.

options.t: A name, a description, and a match rule.
A name and an example value.
options.why: An example helps and it doesn't tell the grader what counts as right.

steps.title: Extract one agreement
steps.teach: Point Claude Code at your schema and at the Northgate agreement. One row per field, following the match rule column.

checks.q: Why extract one agreement before running all four?

options.t: Because the skill isn't written yet.
options.why: True of the ordering and not the reason for it.

options.t: To keep the cost down.
options.why: The cost is small either way. Think about what a first run tells you.

options.t: To find the schema's holes while they're still cheap to fix.

steps.title: Package it as a skill
steps.teach: Turn the working prompt into a file so you can run it again without retyping. Ask Claude Code to write it, and to ask you clarifying questions first.

checks.q: You have a prompt that works. Why turn it into a skill?

options.t: So you can run it again without retyping, the same way every time.
So the model can improve it over time.
options.why: It doesn't change on its own. You change it.

options.t: So it runs faster next time.
options.why: Speed isn't it. Think about what happens the third and fourth time you need it.

checks.q: You ask Claude Code to write the skill file. What should you ask it to do first?

options.t: Show you a draft to approve.
options.why: Useful, and you'd be approving a draft built on its guesses about what you left out.

options.t: Ask you clarifying questions.
Read the schema so it has the context.
options.why: It has that already. What it doesn't have is what you didn't write down.

steps.title: Four agreements, full schedules
steps.teach: Run the skill across all four. One record per agreement, plus the complete charge schedule for each. Not a sample. All of it.

checks.q: Why run every charge schedule rather than a sample of them?

options.t: The skill can't be told to sample.
options.why: It could be. The reason is about what you'd learn rather than what's possible.

options.t: A sample would be faster but less impressive.
options.why: Impressiveness isn't the point of a measurement.

options.t: A sample tells you about the sample. The failures hide in what you skipped.

steps.title: Somebody wrote down the right answer for every field
steps.teach: By hand, checking each value against the document. That is the answer key.

checks.q: The answer key was written by hand, field by field. Why not have Claude produce it?

options.t: You'd be grading its work against its own work.
It isn't accurate enough on this kind of document.
options.why: It may well be accurate. Accuracy isn't what disqualifies it here.

options.t: It would take just as long.
options.why: It would be quicker, which is exactly the temptation. The problem is elsewhere.

steps.title: Score it against the key
steps.teach: Ask Claude Code to compare its output to the answer key, field by field, and report where it matches and where it misses.

checks.q: First scoring run. What does a low score most likely mean at this stage?

options.t: Correct answers are being marked wrong because they're formatted differently.
The answer key has errors in it.
options.why: It might, and that's not what a first uncompared run usually surfaces.

options.t: The extraction is genuinely poor.
options.why: Possible, and there's a much more common explanation on a first comparison.

steps.title: Normalise, then score again
steps.teach: A correct answer can look different from the answer key. Strip the formatting off both sides before you compare.

options.t: Corrects the extraction so it matches the key.
options.why: Nothing about the extraction changes. The comparison changes.

options.t: Strips formatting off both sides before comparing.
Loosens the match so near-misses count as passes.
options.why: That would hide real failures. It removes a difference that was never meaningful.

steps.eyebrow: Exercise 5.3, if you take one thing away
steps.title: You wrote the grader this morning
steps.teach: Everything still failing after normalisation traces back to one field whose match rule was vague, or blank. Open the schema you filled in an hour ago.

checks.q: After normalising, some fields still fail. Where do you look?

options.t: At the prompt, for instructions that contradict each other.
options.why: Worth a look eventually. The rule that decides what counts as correct comes first.

options.t: At the documents, for the cases the model misread.
options.why: You'll find some, and there's a more likely and much cheaper cause first.

options.t: At the schema you filled in this morning, for a vague or blank match rule.

steps.title: Build a scorecard
steps.teach: A wall of pass and fail text is technically an eval and practically useless. You want to look at this and know within three seconds which field is your problem.

checks.q: What makes a scorecard better than a list of passes and failures?

options.t: It can be shared with people who weren't in the session.
options.why: So can a list. The difference is how fast it answers the question.

options.t: It's a more professional deliverable.
options.why: Presentation isn't the reason. Think about what you do with it.

options.t: You can see within three seconds which field is the problem.

steps.title: Fix the specification, never the output
steps.teach: Take the top failing field. Work out which of three things it is, change the rule, and re-run the whole thing.

checks.q: A field keeps failing. What do you change?

options.t: The specification: the rule that says what counts as correct.
The answer key, if the extraction looks defensible.
options.why: Sometimes the key is wrong, and reaching for it first is how a measurement quietly becomes a rubber stamp.

options.t: The output, so it matches the key.
options.why: That fixes one run and teaches you nothing. The next run fails the same way.

steps.title: What this does not give you
steps.teach: A number you trust too much is worse than no number. Five things this class did not teach, and you should know all of them.

checks.q: You have a number. What is it not?

options.t: A way to find which field is weakest.
options.why: It does that well, which is most of why you built it.

options.t: A measure of how well the system will do on documents unlike these four.
A comparison between yesterday's rules and today's.
options.why: That's exactly what it is good for.

checks.q: Why is a number you trust too much worse than no number?

options.t: Because other people will quote it out of context.
options.why: They might, and the first problem is what it does to your own judgement.

options.t: Because it takes effort to produce.
options.why: The effort is worth it. The danger is in what you do with the result.

options.t: Because it stops you looking, and it was only ever measuring what you specified.
